Psalm 91
sahm NINE-tee-one
scripture portion
The ninety-first psalm, known from its opening as “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High”; a psalm of confidence in God’s protection.

📖 Biblical Definition

Psalm 91 is the great psalm of divine protection, a song of confidence in the LORD as the refuge and fortress of His people. It opens with the secret place of the most High and the shadow of the Almighty, and promises deliverance from the snare of the fowler, the noisome pestilence, the terror by night, and the arrow that flieth by day. He that trusts in God shall not be afraid, though a thousand fall at his side, for the LORD is his habitation, and He shall give His angels charge to keep him in all his ways. The psalm must be read with care, for the devil himself quoted its promise of angelic guardianship when he tempted Christ to cast Himself from the temple, and the Lord answered, “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” The promise is not a charm against all bodily harm, nor a license to presume upon God, but the covenant assurance that no evil shall finally befall the one who dwells in God—that the believer is kept for an end, body and soul, in life and in death. The dictionary receives Psalm 91 as the believer’s confidence in the particular providence of God, rightly understood: not exemption from all suffering, but the certainty that the saint is hidden in the Almighty and shall be brought safely home.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The psalm of divine protection, confessing the LORD as refuge and fortress; rightly read not as a charm against all harm but as covenant assurance that no evil shall finally befall the believer.

expand to see more

PSALM 91, the psalm of confidence in God’s protection.

Opens with the secret place of the most High and the shadow of the Almighty.

Promises deliverance from the snare, the pestilence, the terror by night, the arrow by day.

Its angel promise was quoted by Satan in tempting Christ, and answered by Him.

Assures not exemption from suffering but that no evil shall finally befall the believer.

📖 Key Scripture

Psa 91:1 — "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."

Psa 91:2 — "I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust."

Psa 91:11 — "For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways."

Mat 4:7 — "Jesus said unto him, It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The psalm is twisted into a guarantee of bodily safety or a magic charm, the very presumption the devil urged on Christ.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right reading of the promise. Satan himself quoted Psalm 91 to tempt the Lord to a presumptuous leap, and Christ refused: to claim God’s protection while running into needless danger is not faith but tempting God. The psalm assures the believer who dwells in God, walks in his appointed ways, and trusts the Almighty—not the presumptuous who demand exemption from all harm on their own terms.

Where a corruption presses, it is the health-and-prosperity misuse that reads the psalm as a blanket guarantee against sickness, accident, and death. Saints have suffered and died trusting these very words; martyrs have gone to the stake with Psalm 91 on their lips. The promise is deeper than the body’s safety: no evil shall finally befall the one who is hidden in God, for even death is swallowed up in the keeping of the Almighty, and the believer is brought through every danger safely home.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The psalm’s images of refuge, fortress, and shadow gather the covenant assurance of dwelling safely in God.

expand to see more

Hebrew maḥseh — a refuge, shelter, place of safety; “he is my refuge.”

Hebrew metsudah — a fortress, stronghold; the LORD as the believer’s defense.

Hebrew tsel — shadow, shade; “the shadow of the Almighty,” nearness and covering.

Hebrew Shadday — the Almighty, the all-sufficient God.

The angelic charge of verse 11 is cited and rightly bounded by Christ in the wilderness.

Usage

"Psalm 91 is a favorite of soldiers and the persecuted for its confidence in God’s keeping."

"Christ’s answer to Satan’s misuse of it guards against presuming upon God."

"It is preached as covenant assurance, not a guarantee of bodily exemption from suffering."
